questions.q: Why can immediate, unlimited retries make an outage worse rather than better?
options: Retries always consume more Apex callout limits than the original request
If the target system is already struggling under load, a flood of immediate retries adds more load to the exact system that's already failing, instead of giving it room to recover
Immediate retries are blocked by Salesforce's platform automatically
Retries can only be configured to run once per day
questions.explain: Retrying immediately and repeatedly piles additional load onto a system that's already struggling, which is the opposite of what's needed -- exponential backoff exists specifically to avoid this.

questions.q: What is a dead-letter queue, and why does Doverfield's design use one?
options: A queue of messages that have already been successfully processed
A holding area for messages that exhausted their retry attempts without success, so a human or automated alert can investigate rather than the message silently vanishing
A backup copy of every successful ERP sync message
A Salesforce feature that disables failed Apex triggers permanently
questions.explain: Without a dead-letter queue, a design either retries forever or silently drops the failed message -- the dead-letter queue gives failures a visible, recoverable home instead of either bad outcome.

questions.q: Why is idempotency a precondition for safe retry logic, per this lesson?
options: Idempotency has nothing to do with retry safety

If an operation isn't idempotent, retrying a call that actually succeeded the first time (but whose confirmation was lost) could create a duplicate record on the retry, rather than safely reapplying the same result
Idempotent operations cannot be retried at all
Idempotency only matters for read-only queries, never for writes
questions.explain: A retry is only safe if repeating it produces the same outcome as running it once -- upsert on a stable External ID provides exactly that property for Doverfield's order-creation sync.

questions.q: What category of failure does a scheduled reconciliation job catch that retry logic and dead-letter queues don't?
options: Failures where a message was silently lost before reaching the retry logic, or where a bug produced incorrect data without technically triggering a failure
Failures that occur more than once per second
Only failures that have already been logged in the dead-letter queue
Reconciliation jobs catch exactly the same failures as retry logic, just later
questions.explain: Reconciliation is a second, independent safety net specifically because some drift never trips the retry/dead-letter mechanisms at all -- it compares actual record state on a periodic cadence instead.

questions.q: What makes Doverfield's retry pattern 'exponential backoff' specifically, rather than simple retry?
options: It retries exactly once, with no further attempts
It waits a progressively longer interval before each successive retry attempt, up to a capped maximum number of attempts
It retries only during business hours
It doubles the number of callouts made on each retry attempt
questions.explain: Exponential backoff's defining feature is increasing the wait time between successive attempts, capped at a maximum, rather than retrying at a constant interval or retrying indefinitely.
